fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: The 200-File PR No One Could Review
fieldNotes.source: Staff engineer at Vyapar Forge, a Hyderabad-based series-C developer-tooling company
fieldNotes.story:
On a Friday in late March 2026, a Vyapar engineer kicked off an autonomous Claude Code run with a single prompt: *"Migrate our monolith from REST to gRPC. Take your time."* He gave it Opus 4.7 with the 1M-context window, MCP access to the repo, and went home for the weekend. He returned Monday to a **6-hour, 2.4M-token session** that had produced exactly what he asked for: a single PR, **207 files changed, +18,400 / -14,200 lines.**

It compiled. Most of the tests passed. It was, by any reasonable definition, the migration. It was also **completely unreviewable**. The senior engineer assigned the review opened the PR, scrolled for 90 seconds, closed the tab, and posted in #engineering: *"I cannot in good conscience approve this. Splitting it would take a week. Reviewing it line-by-line would take a month."*

The PR sat for 11 days. Eventually the team **closed it without merging** and rebuilt the migration from scratch using **bounded subagent tasks**: one service per subagent, ~15-30 file PRs, sequential merges, each reviewable in 30 minutes. Total elapsed time: 4 weeks. **Total reviewable PRs: 23.** Total merged: 23. Total trust intact.

The 6-hour autonomous run is now an in-house cautionary tale. Every Vyapar engineer who joins gets shown the screenshot of the closed PR.
fieldNotes.takeaway: Long autonomous runs produce work, not reviewable work. Bounded subagents with tight artifacts are how you actually ship at scale — the constraint is *human review capacity*, not *model capacity*.

bossBattle.title: Boss Battle: Week 14 — The TypeScript 6.0 Migration Fanout
bossBattle.setup:
**Week 14 of Q2 2026.** The Claude rollout is mostly stuck across Velora — coding, cowork, design. Last big task before quarter-end review: **migrate 14 microservices from TypeScript 5.4 to TypeScript 6.0.** Each service is 5k-40k lines, owned by 2-3 engineers, with non-trivial typing changes (the new `satisfies` semantics, narrowed `unknown`, stricter generic inference).

You — Karthik — have **two weeks**, **a budget of ~5M Claude tokens**, and a CTO who will personally read whatever ships. Get the design wrong and you produce a Vyapar-style 200-file disaster in 14 services at once.

coach.name: Anthropic-Veteran Anuj
coach.role: Has orchestrated three production migrations using subagent fanouts, two of which actually worked

stages.prompt: Anuj draws a whiteboard. *"First decision. **One big run, or many small ones?**"*

options.label: One big Opus 4.7 run, 1M-context, all 14 services in one session — the model can hold it all.
options.explain: This is exactly the Vyapar mistake at 14x scale. Even if the model can hold it, *humans cannot review it*. You'd produce one unreviewable PR per service, simultaneously. Disaster.

options.label: **14 parallel subagent tasks**, one per service, each with its own bounded `CLAUDE.md` and a 30-min-reviewable PR target.
options.explain: **Right architecture.** Subagents map cleanly to services. Reviewable-PR-as-constraint is the load-bearing rule. Anuj draws a green tick.

options.label: Sequential one-at-a-time runs across 14 services — safest, slowest.
options.explain: Sequential is *safer per task* but burns the entire two-week budget on serial latency. You have parallelism available; use it for the 11 services that don't share dependencies.

options.label: Parallel for the 11 independent services, **sequential for the 3 that share the auth library** (which itself needs migrating first).
options.explain: **Top-tier.** You correctly identified the dependency graph. Auth library migrates first (sequential), then 11 leaf services in parallel, then the 3 dependent services. This is the actual production-shaped plan.

stages.prompt: **Subagent design.** Each fanned-out task gets a prompt + context. **What goes in?**

options.label: *"Migrate this service to TypeScript 6.0."* + the repo path. That's it.
options.explain: No scope, no PR-size cap, no review hooks. The subagent will produce the Vyapar-shaped output: technically correct, operationally unmergeable.

options.label: Migration brief + service `CLAUDE.md` + an explicit **PR-size budget** ('split into PRs of ≤25 files; each must pass typecheck independently') + a **handoff artifact** (migration log written to `docs/MIGRATIONS/`).
options.explain: **This is the recipe.** PR-size budget enforces reviewability. Independent typecheck enforces incremental safety. The handoff artifact lets the next subagent (or human) pick up the thread without rerunning context.

options.label: Migration brief + a stern warning: 'Do not over-refactor.'
options.explain: Stern warnings without structural enforcement are decorative. The subagent needs *constraints*, not *requests*. PR-size budget is a constraint; 'don't over-refactor' is a hope.

options.label: Migration brief + service `CLAUDE.md` + PR-size budget + handoff artifact + **a checkpoint at each PR**: the subagent stops and waits for human approval before continuing.
options.explain: **Top-tier paranoia, correctly applied.** Checkpoints turn a 6-hour autonomous run into a 6-hour *supervised* run. You catch wrong-turn behavior at PR 1, not at PR 23.

stages.prompt: **Model picks.** You have Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5 in the menu. **Which goes where?**

options.label: Opus 4.7 for everything — best model wins.
options.explain: You'd burn the 5M-token budget in 4 services and run dry. Opus is the right tool for *hard reasoning*, not for *applying a known migration to leaf code*.

options.label: **Opus 4.7** for the auth-library migration (hard, dependency-heavy, sets pattern). **Sonnet 4.6** for the 11 leaf services (apply known pattern). **Haiku 4.5** for repetitive cleanup (lint fixes, import reordering).
options.explain: **Exactly the cost-shape that works.** Reserve the most capable model for the load-bearing decision; let the cheaper models do the high-volume known work. This is how you stay inside 5M tokens.

options.label: Haiku 4.5 for everything — cheapest, fastest.
options.explain: Haiku will produce confidently-wrong type narrowing on the new `satisfies` semantics in three services. Cost-optimization without capability-matching is false economy.

options.label: Opus 4.7 for auth + the 3 dependent services. Sonnet 4.6 for the 11 leaves. **Skip Haiku** — too risky on type-system work.
options.explain: **Defensible.** TypeScript 6.0 type changes are subtle enough that you may not want Haiku in the loop at all. Higher per-token cost, but lower review burden. Anuj approves either of the two splits depending on team comfort.

stages.prompt: **Handoff design.** When a subagent finishes its service, what does it produce so the *next step* (human review, dependent-service subagent) can pick up cleanly?

options.label: Just the PR — the diff is the artifact.
options.explain: Diff-only handoffs lose the *reasoning*: why this approach over the alternative, what edge cases it punted on, what tests don't yet cover. Reviewers re-derive context that the subagent already had.

options.label: A `docs/MIGRATIONS/<service>.md` written by the subagent: scope, approach taken, decisions deferred, tests added, **known gaps**, suggested follow-up. Plus the PR.
options.explain: **The full handoff.** Reviewer reads the migration doc in 4 minutes, then reviews the PR in 25, total 30. Future engineer hitting an edge case 6 months later finds the 'known gaps' section. This is the artifact that makes the rollout *cumulative*.

options.label: PR + a Slack message in #engineering summarizing what the subagent did.
options.explain: Slack messages are ephemeral. In 6 weeks the channel will have scrolled past, and the migration context will live nowhere durable. Use docs, not chat.

options.label: Handoff doc + PR + **automated checkpoint**: the next dependent-service subagent reads the upstream service's migration doc as part of its context window.
options.explain: **Top-tier.** This is the orchestration pattern that compounds: each subagent builds on the last one's *learnings*, not just its *output*. By service 14, you've encoded 13 services' worth of edge cases.

outcomes.perfect: You designed a real production fanout: dependency-aware ordering, model-tier matching, PR-size budgets, handoff artifacts, and checkpoints. **23 reviewable PRs land in two weeks**, the CTO reads three of them and stops there because they're boring in the best way. Velora's Q2 review goes well. **Anuj quietly forwards your design doc to the Anthropic team as a customer reference.**
outcomes.good: You got the architecture mostly right but cut a corner on either model selection or handoff design. Re-read the lesson on **bounded subagents** — the difference between 23 reviewable PRs and 1 Vyapar PR is in the artifacts, not the model.
outcomes.learn: You either built one giant unreviewable run, or you parallelized without thinking through dependencies and produced 14 conflicting PRs. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **PR-size budgets**, **dependency-aware fanout**, and **handoff artifacts**. The constraint is human review capacity, always.
